title:
Lü Bu helps Wang Yun and cuts down a tyrant
Li Jue heeds Jia Xu and falls upon Chang'an
paragraphs: Now the man who had knocked [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) down was [Li Ru](char-li-ru). He raised him up and brought him into the study, and there they sat. Dong Zhuo said: "What brought you here?" Li Ru said: "I had just reached the gate when I heard that you had gone into the back garden in anger, looking for [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu). I hurried after you, and met him running out, crying: 'The Grand Preceptor means to kill me!' I ran into the garden to make peace, and blundered against you, my lord. I have earned death by it!" Dong Zhuo said: "The traitor is not to be borne! He toyed with my own concubine, and I swear I will have his life!" Li Ru said: "You are wrong there, my lord. At [the feast of the broken cap-strings](misc-broken-cap-strings), King Zhuang of Chu would not call Jiang Xiong to account for toying with his own favorite, and afterwards, when the Qin troops had him hemmed in, it was Jiang Xiong who fought to the death to save him. [Diaochan](char-diaochan) is no more than a woman, but Lü Bu is your own right hand and a bold captain. Take this chance and give her to him, and he will be so moved by the favor that he will repay you with his life. I beg you to think well on it." Dong Zhuo brooded a long while, then said: "There is reason in what you say. I will think of it."

[Li Ru](char-li-ru) thanked him and withdrew. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) went into the back hall, called [Diaochan](char-diaochan) and asked her: "What is this intrigue of yours with [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)?" Diaochan said weeping: "I was in the back garden looking at the flowers when Lü Bu came on me suddenly. I was starting away from him in fright when he said: 'I am the Grand Preceptor's son. Why run from me?' Then he took up his halberd and drove me as far as the Fengyi Pavilion. I saw that his mind was impure, and feared he would force me, so I would have thrown myself into the lotus pool and made an end of it, but the wretch caught me in his arms. I hung between life and death until you came and saved me." Dong Zhuo said: "What if I were to give you to Lü Bu?" Diaochan cried out in dismay: "I have served a man of rank, and now I am to be handed down to a household slave. I will die before I bear that shame!" And she snatched the fine sword that hung on the wall to cut her own throat.

That same day [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) gave the order to return to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), and the whole body of officials bowed him away. [Diaochan](char-diaochan), from the carriage, saw [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) far off in the press of people with his eyes on her, and half covered her face as though she were weeping bitterly. When the carriage had gone far, Lü Bu drew his rein on a knoll and watched the dust of it, sighing in grief and bitterness. Then he heard a man behind him ask: "[Marquis of Wen](char-lu-bu), why do you not follow the Grand Preceptor, but stand here gazing after him and sighing?" Lü Bu turned, and it was [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), the Minister of the Masses.

When they had greeted each other [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said: "It is long since I saw you, General, for a slight sickness has kept my doors shut these days past. Today, with [the Grand Preceptor](char-dong-zhuo)'s carriage going back to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), I had to come out, ill as I am, to see him away, and I count it a piece of luck to have met you. Tell me, what sets you sighing here?" [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) said: "It is [your daughter](char-diaochan) that I sigh for." Wang Yun feigned surprise. "All this while, and she is not yours yet, General?" Lü Bu said: "The old traitor has had her to himself this long while!" Wang Yun made a great show of astonishment. "I cannot believe such a thing!" Then Lü Bu told him the whole story. Wang Yun turned his face up and stamped his foot, and for a good space said nothing; at length he spoke: "I never thought the Grand Preceptor would do a thing so beastly!" And he took Lü Bu by the hand. "Come to my humble house, and we will talk of it." Lü Bu went home with him. Wang Yun led him into an inner room and set wine before him, and Lü Bu told over again, at length, what had passed at the Fengyi Pavilion. Wang Yun said: "The Grand Preceptor has defiled my daughter and robbed you of your wife, General, and the realm will laugh — not at him, but at you and me! I am old and worthless, and no more need be said of me. But that you, the hero of the age, should bear such shame!"

[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s anger blazed up, and he struck the table with a shout. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said quickly: "My loose tongue is at fault, General. Let your anger cool." Lü Bu said: "I swear I will kill the old traitor and wipe out my shame!" Wang Yun clapped a hand over his mouth. "Say no more, General. I fear it will fall upon me as well." Lü Bu said: "Shall a man live stifled under another all his days?" Wang Yun said: "With such gifts, you are indeed no man for [the Grand Preceptor Dong](char-dong-zhuo) to hold within bounds." Lü Bu said: "I would kill the old traitor, but we stand as father and son, and I fear what later men would say of it." Wang Yun smiled a little. "Your own surname is Lü, General, and the Grand Preceptor's is Dong. Where was the love of father and son when he threw the halberd at you?" Lü Bu started up. "But for your words, Minister, I had near led myself astray!"

[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) saw that his mind was made up, and pressed him: "If you, General, uphold the house of Han you are a loyal servant, and your name shall go down in the histories and the fragrance of it last a hundred ages; if you help [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) you are a traitor, and the historian's brush will leave your stench to all the ages after." [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) rose from his mat and bowed to the ground. "My mind is made up, Minister. Have no doubt of me." Wang Yun said: "I fear only that it may fail, and bring a great calamity on us instead." Then Lü Bu drew the blade at his belt, pricked his arm and swore upon the blood. Wang Yun knelt and thanked him. "If the altars of Han still stand, it will be of your giving, General. Let nothing leak out! When the hour comes I shall have a plan, and will send you word."

[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) gave his word readily and went. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) then called in Shisun Rui, Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat, and Huang Wan, Director of Retainers, to take counsel with him. Shisun Rui said: "His Majesty is but newly recovered of his sickness. Send a man with a ready tongue to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), that he may ask [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) in for a council. At the same time put a secret edict of the Son of Heaven into Lü Bu's hands, and let him set armed men within the palace gate, so that Dong Zhuo is cut down as he is brought in. That is the best course." Huang Wan said: "Who will dare to go?" Shisun Rui said: "[Li Su](char-li-su), the Cavalry Commandant, is of Lü Bu's own commandery, and carries a grudge that Dong Zhuo has never advanced him. Send that man, and Dong Zhuo will suspect nothing." Wang Yun approved, and he had Lü Bu called in to the council. Lü Bu said: "It was this same man who talked me into killing [Ding Jianyang](char-ding-yuan). If he will not go, I will have his head first." So they sent secretly for Li Su, and he came.

[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) said: "In other days you talked me into killing [Ding Jianyang](char-ding-yuan) and going over to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). Now Dong Zhuo cheats the Son of Heaven above and grinds the people below, his guilt is brimming over, and the wrath of gods and men alike is on him. Carry the edict of the Son of Heaven to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu) and summon him to court. We will lay men in wait to cut him down, prop up the house of Han, and be loyal servants together. What do you say?" [Li Su](char-li-su) said: "I have long wished to be rid of the traitor, and only grieved that I had no man of like mind. Now that you are resolved, General, it is Heaven's gift. How should I dare prove false?" And he broke an arrow in pledge. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said: "Carry this through, sir, and you need not doubt of high office."

Next day [Li Su](char-li-su) rode to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu) with a dozen horsemen. Word was brought that an edict had come from the Son of Heaven, and [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had him called in. Li Su entered and bowed. Dong Zhuo said: "What edict has the Son of Heaven sent?" Li Su said: "The Son of Heaven is newly healed of his sickness, and the edict calls the civil and military officers together in the Weiyang Hall, to deliberate upon yielding the throne to you, Grand Preceptor." Dong Zhuo said: "And what does [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) say to it?" Li Su said: "Minister Wang has set men to build the Terrace of Abdication already, and waits only for you to come, my lord." Dong Zhuo was overjoyed. "Last night I dreamed that a dragon covered my body, and here is the good news. The hour must not be let slip!" So he ordered his four trusted generals, [Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou), to hold Meiwu with three thousand of the Feixiong troops, and that same day set his train in order to return to the capital. Turning to Li Su he said: "When I am Emperor, you shall be the Bearer of the Mace." Li Su bowed his thanks and called himself his subject.

[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) went in to take leave of his mother, who was then past ninety. She asked: "Where are you going, my son?" Dong Zhuo said: "Your son goes to receive the throne of Han, and before long you will be the Empress Dowager!" His mother said: "These days my flesh has quivered and my heart has started in me. I fear it is no good omen." Dong Zhuo said: "You are to be the mother of the realm. Great news must have its forewarnings!" So he took his leave. As he was setting out he said to [Diaochan](char-diaochan): "When I am Son of Heaven, I will make you Noble Consort." Diaochan, who knew well enough how the matter stood, feigned delight and bowed her thanks.

[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) came out of the stronghold and took his carriage, with his escort before and behind, and set out for [Chang'an](loc-changan). He had not gone thirty li when a wheel of the carriage broke, so he got down and took to horse. Before another ten li the horse screamed and plunged and snapped its bridle. Dong Zhuo asked [Li Su](char-li-su): "A wheel broken, a bridle parted. What omen is this?" Li Su said: "It is the omen that you are to receive the throne of Han, Grand Preceptor, putting off the old for the new, and that you will ride hereafter in a jade carriage and on a golden saddle." Dong Zhuo was pleased and believed him.

Next day, as they went, a wild wind sprang up of a sudden and a dark mist hid the sky. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) asked [Li Su](char-li-su): "What sign is this?" Li Su said: "You are to mount the dragon throne, my lord, and there must be red light and purple mist to set off the majesty of Heaven." Again Dong Zhuo was pleased and doubted nothing. When he came to the city the whole body of officials came out to meet him. Only [Li Ru](char-li-ru) lay sick at home and could not come. Dong Zhuo went on to the Chancellor's residence, and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came in to congratulate him. Dong Zhuo said: "When I come to the throne you shall command all the armies of the realm." Lü Bu bowed his thanks and lay down for the night before Dong Zhuo's tent. That night a dozen children were singing out beyond the walls, and the wind carried the song into the tent:
> A thousand li of grass,
> How green it grows!
> Ten days are up above,
> No life it knows! [*](misc-childrens-rhyme-ch9-p13)
The tune was mournful. Dong Zhuo asked Li Su: "What does it foretell, good or ill?" Li Su said: "It means only that the house of Liu falls and the house of Dong rises."

At dawn next day [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) set his train in order and went up to court. On the way he saw a Daoist in a blue robe and a white headcloth, holding a long pole with a strip of cloth a zhang long bound to it, and at either end of the cloth was written the character for "mouth" [*](misc-daoists-warning-ch9-p14). Dong Zhuo asked [Li Su](char-li-su): "What does the Daoist mean by that?" Li Su said: "Must be a crazy man." And he called the guard to drive him off. Dong Zhuo went on to the court, where the officers in their court robes met and saluted him along the road, while Li Su walked beside the carriage with a sword in his hand. At the Northern Side Gate the soldiers were all held outside, and only the twenty-odd men of the carriage went in with him. Dong Zhuo saw from afar [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) and the others standing at the door of the hall, each with a sword in his hand, and asked Li Su in alarm: "What do the swords mean?"

[Li Su](char-li-su) made no answer, but pushed the carriage straight in. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) cried aloud: "The traitor is here! Where are the guards?" A hundred men and more came out from either side, with halberds and leveled lances, and thrust at him. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) wore mail beneath his robe and the points would not go through, but he took a wound in the arm and fell from the carriage, crying: "Where is my son [Fengxian](char-lu-bu)?" [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came out from behind the carriage and said: "By edict I strike the traitor down!" One thrust of the halberd went clean through the throat, and Li Su had the head off in his hand. Then Lü Bu held the halberd in his left hand, drew the edict from his breast with his right, and shouted: "By edict the traitor Dong Zhuo is put down. No other man shall be questioned!" And the officers all cheered. Later men made a poem in lament for Dong Zhuo:
> Had it gone through, the throne had been his seat;
> Had it gone wrong, a rich man's safe retreat.
> Who knew that Heaven keeps no partial way?
> [Meiwu](loc-meiwu) scarce finished, he in ruin lay.

Now [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) raised his voice: "It was [Li Ru](char-li-ru) who helped [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) to all his cruelties! Who will take him?" [Li Su](char-li-su) answered that he would go. Then a shouting was heard outside the palace gate, and word came that Li Ru's own servants had bound him and brought him in. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) had him taken bound to the market place and beheaded, and Dong Zhuo's body set up in the open street for a warning. The body was so fat that the soldiers who watched it put a light in the navel for a lamp, and the grease ran over the ground. All who passed flung the head about with their hands and trod the body under their feet. Wang Yun further ordered Lü Bu, with [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) and Li Su, to take fifty thousand men to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), seize Dong Zhuo's goods and household, and set them down in a register.

Now [Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou), hearing that [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was dead and that [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was on his way, led off the Feixiong troops and rode through the night for [Liang Province](loc-liang-province). Lü Bu came to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), and his first act was to take [Diaochan](char-diaochan). [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) gave orders that the children shut up in the stronghold should all be set free. But every kinsman of Dong Zhuo's, old and young alike, was put to death, including his mother. His brother [Dong Min](char-dong-min) and his nephew [Dong Huang](char-dong-huang) were beheaded and their heads set up. They registered what was hoarded in the stronghold — some hundreds of thousands in gold, with silks and pearls, jewels and vessels and grain past all counting — and brought back their report to [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun). He feasted the soldiers richly and laid out a banquet in the hall of state, where he gathered the officers together and they drank to the victory.

In the midst of the feasting word was brought: "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s body lies exposed in the market, and a man has thrown himself upon it and weeps aloud." [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said angrily: "Dong Zhuo has met his punishment, and every gentleman and commoner rejoices in it. Who is this, that dares to weep over him?" And he called the guards: "Bring him before me!"

In a little while the man was brought in, and all the officers started at the sight of him, for it was [Cai Yong](char-cai-yong), the Palace Attendant. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) rebuked him: "The traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has met his punishment this day, and it is a great good fortune for the state. You are a servant of Han. Why do you not rejoice with the rest, but weep instead over a traitor?" Cai Yong owned his fault. "I have little ability, but I know what righteousness asks, and would never turn my back on the state for Dong Zhuo's sake. It was only that for a moment I remembered that he had known my worth, and the tears came before I was aware of it. I know the fault is great. Brand my face and cut off my feet if it must be, but let me finish the history of Han and atone for my guilt by it, and I shall count myself fortunate."

The officers, who valued [Cai Yong](char-cai-yong)'s gifts, all pleaded hard for him, and [Ma Midi](char-ma-midi), the Grand Tutor, said privately to [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun): "[Bojie](char-cai-yong)'s talent is unequaled in the age. Let him finish the history of Han, and it will be a glorious work. His filial conduct, besides, has long been famous, and if you kill him out of hand you will lose the goodwill of men." Wang Yun said: "Emperor Wu of old did not put Sima Qian to death, but set him to write his history, and a book of slanders has come down to later ages for it. The fortunes of the state are low now and the government in disorder, and we cannot have a flatterer holding the brush at the young sovereign's elbow, to leave us under his sneers." Ma Midi went out without a word, and said in private to the rest: "Wang Yun will leave no posterity! Good men are the mainstay of a state, and their writings are its law. Destroy the mainstay and throw away the law, and how shall the state stand long?"

Now [Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) had fled to Shaanxi and settled there, and they sent a man to [Chang'an](loc-changan) with a memorial asking pardon. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said: "In every evil of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s these four had a hand. All others in the realm shall be pardoned, but not these four." The messenger carried word back to Li Jue, who said: "If no pardon is to be had, let each man flee for his life." Then [Jia Xu](char-jia-xu), his counselor, said: "If you abandon your men and travel alone, a mere village chief could put you in bonds. Better draw the men of Shaanxi together, join them to your own companies, and cut your way into Chang'an to avenge Dong Zhuo. If we carry it through we shall hold the court and set the realm in order, and if we are beaten it will not be too late to run then."

[Li Jue](char-li-jue) and the rest thought well of this, and set a rumor going through [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) that [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) meant to sweep the region clean of its people. Fear ran through them all. Then the four declared: "Rather than die for nothing, will you follow us and rise?" And every man was willing. So they gathered more than a hundred thousand, divided them into four columns, and came driving upon [Chang'an](loc-changan). On the road they met [Niu Fu](char-niu-fu), [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s son-in-law and a General of the Household, with five thousand men, on his way to avenge his wife's father. Li Jue joined forces with him and set him in the van, and the four came on one behind another.

[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) heard that the [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) troops were coming, and took counsel with [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu). Lü Bu said: "Rest easy, Minister. Such rats are of no account!" So he took [Li Su](char-li-su) and led the army out against them. Li Su led the van and came face to face with [Niu Fu](char-niu-fu), and there was a great slaughter. Niu Fu, unable to stand against him, drew off beaten. But that night, at the second watch, Niu Fu stormed his camp and caught him unready. Li Su's men broke and scattered, and he fled above thirty li and lost more than half his force before he came in to Lü Bu. Lü Bu shouted: "How dare you break the spirit of my army!" And he had Li Su beheaded and the head hung up at the gate of the camp.

Next day [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) brought his men up against [Niu Fu](char-niu-fu). And how should Niu Fu stand against him? He was heavily beaten again and fled. That night he called in Hu Chi'er, a man he trusted, and said: "Lü Bu is too bold and too strong, and there is no standing against him. Better keep it from [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and the other three, take the gold and pearls, and leave the army with a few of our own people." Hu Chi'er agreed, and that same night they gathered the gold and pearls and went out of the camp with three or four in their train. They were about to cross a river when Hu Chi'er, coveting the treasure, killed Niu Fu and carried the head to Lü Bu. Lü Bu asked how it had come about, and the men of the party informed against him: "Hu Chi'er murdered Niu Fu to get his gold and jewels." Lü Bu was incensed, and had Hu Chi'er put to death on the spot. Then he led his men forward and came full upon Li Jue's companies, and before they formed he leveled his halberd, put his horse at them and waved his men on. Li Jue's troops could not withstand the charge, and fell back above fifty li and made their camp against a hill. There Li Jue called in [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou), and said: "Lü Bu is brave but no strategist, and we need not fear him. I will hold the mouth of the valley with my men and draw him out to fight every day. You, General Guo, take your men round and strike at his rear the way [Peng Yue](char-peng-yue) harried Chu, sounding the gongs to advance and beating the drums to draw off. And you two, Zhang Ji and Fan Chou, divide your men into two columns and make straight for [Chang'an](loc-changan). He cannot guard front and rear at once, and he will be soundly beaten." And they all took his plan.

Now [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) drew up his men below the hill, and [Li Jue](char-li-jue) led his out to offer battle. Lü Bu charged in a rage, and Li Jue fell back up the slope. Arrows and stones came down from the hill like rain, and Lü Bu's men could not advance. Then word came that [Guo Si](char-guo-si) was cutting in at the rear, so Lü Bu turned hastily to meet him, but the drums rolled out and Guo Si's men had drawn off already. He was just calling his own men back when the gongs sounded and Li Jue's came on again, and before he could close with them Guo Si was at his back once more. Then, when Lü Bu turned upon Guo Si, the drums beat and he was gone, until Lü Bu's breast was bursting with rage. So it went for several days, and he could neither force them to a battle nor get any rest.

While [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was still fuming a rider came at speed with word that [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) had fallen upon [Chang'an](loc-changan) with their two columns, and that the capital was in grave danger. He hurried back with his men, and [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) came cutting in behind him. With no mind to stand and fight he only pressed on, losing a good many men and horses. By the time he came under the walls of Chang'an the rebels lay thick about it as clouds and rain, with the city ringed round, and his troops fared badly in the fighting. His own soldiers feared his harsh and violent temper, and many of them went over to the rebels, which troubled Lü Bu greatly.

Some days later [Li Meng](char-li-meng) and [Wang Fang](char-wang-fang), remnants of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s party, turned traitor within the city and opened a gate by stealth, and the four rebel columns poured in together. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) charged this way and that but could not hold them. With some hundreds of horse he rode to the Qingsuo Gate and called to [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun): "Things are desperate! Mount, Minister, and come out through the pass with me, and we will look for a better way." Wang Yun said: "If the altars of the land lend us their power and the state can be set at peace, that is all I wish for. If it may not be, I will lay down my life. I will not run from danger to save myself. Carry my farewell to the lords east of the pass, and bid them strive with the state ever in their thoughts!"

[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) urged him again and again, but [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) would not go. Before long the flames at every gate were going up to the sky, and Lü Bu had no choice but to leave his household behind and gallop out through the pass with a hundred horse and more, to take refuge with [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu). [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) loosed their troops to plunder, and Chong Fu the Minister of Ceremonies, Lu Kui the Minister Coachman, Zhou Huan the Grand Herald, Cui Lie the Colonel of the City Gates and Wang Qi the Colonel of Picked Cavalry all died in the calamity that fell upon the state. The rebels pressed hard about the inner court, and the attendants begged the Son of Heaven to go up on the Xuanping Gate and quiet the tumult. When Li Jue and the rest saw the yellow canopy they held their men back and cried: "Long live [the Emperor](char-prince-xie)!" [Emperor Xian](char-prince-xie) leaned from the tower and asked: "You did not wait for leave, but entered [Chang'an](loc-changan) on your own authority. What do you mean to do?" Li Jue and Guo Si looked up and answered: "[The Grand Preceptor Dong](char-dong-zhuo) was a pillar of Your Majesty's state, and Wang Yun murdered him without cause. We have come only to avenge him, and would not dare rebel. Let us but see Wang Yun, and we will draw our men off."

[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) was at [the Emperor](char-prince-xie)'s side, and hearing this he said: "What I did, I did for the altars of the land. It has come to this now, and Your Majesty must not ruin the state to spare me. Let me go down to the two traitors." The Emperor wavered, unable to bear it. Then Wang Yun leaped from the tower of the Xuanping Gate and cried aloud: "Wang Yun is here!" [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) drew their swords and shouted at him: "What was the Grand Preceptor's crime, that he should be killed?" Wang Yun said: "The crimes of the traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) filled heaven and spanned the earth beyond all telling. On the day he was put to death every gentleman and commoner of [Chang'an](loc-changan) rejoiced together. Have you alone not heard?" Li Jue and Guo Si said: "Say the Grand Preceptor was guilty. What was our crime, that you would not pardon us?" Wang Yun cursed them: "Rebels! Why so many words? I, Wang Yun, am ready to die today!" The two traitors raised their hands and killed him there below the tower. A historian wrote a poem in his praise:
> When Wang Yun set his stratagem in play,
> The traitor Dong Zhuo's power passed away.
> He bore his country's grief within his breast,
> And on his brow the cares of court were pressed.
> A noble spirit scaled the heavens' height,
> And loyalty struck through the stars of night.
> His soul and spirit to this very hour
> Go circling still about the Phoenix Tower.

The rebels, having killed [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), sent men to put his whole kindred to death, old and young alike, and every gentleman and commoner wept for them. Then [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) reasoned together: "We have come this far. If we do not kill the Son of Heaven and strike for the great prize now, when shall we?" And sword in hand, with a great shout, they forced their way within. Truly:
> The chief offender paid, the scourge scarce past,
> His creatures range at large, and woe comes fast.
What came of [Emperor Xian](char-prince-xie)'s life, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: the feast of the broken cap-strings
versions.description: A tale told of King Zhuang of Chu. At a night feast for his ministers the lamps blew out, and in the dark one of them laid hands on the king's favorite concubine; she tore the string from his cap, so that the light should show who it was. But the king had every man at the table break his own cap-string before the lamps were lit again, and never asked. Years afterward, in a difficult battle, that man fought to the death to save him.

versions.name: the children's rhyme

versions.name: the Daoist's warning
versions.description: A riddle in written characters: two "mouth" (口) set one above the other make Lü (呂), and the cloth (布) they are written on gives Bu, naming [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu).
